tagline: Ferries and a fur-trading post shaped journeys beside the Snake River.
intro: The Snake River places Homedale on the boundary between Owyhee and Canyon counties. Sunnyslope is a center of the Snake River Valley wine region, with State Highway 55 passing through the community.

River crossings once connected mines with rail transport. In 1884, J. C. Bernard began a ferry and opened a road between Silver City and Caldwell’s Oregon Short Line railhead. Stagecoach and freight traffic used the road and ferry; a bridge at Walter’s Ferry in 1920 ended Bernard’s period of success.

Parma has a reconstructed Fort Boise, while Homedale’s own ferry history began in 1898. At Claytonia, a former railway gravel pit became a pond and fish habitat. Farther south, State Highway 45 reaches the riverside community of Walters Ferry near the highway’s southern end.

moments.title: Parma
moments.text: Parma’s Fort Boise is a reconstruction; the old trading-post site lies within the Fort Boise Wildlife Management Area. Thomas McKay built Fort Boise in 1834 with Hudson’s Bay Company backing to challenge the American Fort Hall farther east. The company took full control in 1836. Francois Payette built a second Fort Boise near the Boise–Snake confluence in 1838, with a pole stockade later covered and replaced by sun-dried adobe. A different Fort Boise, established as a military post in 1863, stood fifty miles east, at the place that became the city of Boise.

moments.title: Homedale
moments.text: Jacob Mussell’s ferry made Homedale easier to reach across the Snake River in 1898. By 1914, the settlement had a railroad, schoolhouse, mayor and council, six years before it became an official city. The railroad connection made Homedale a terminus of an Oregon Short Line branch. Austrians arriving in 1914 had been promised good farmland but found undeveloped land they still had to purchase. An Austrian Town remains in Homedale. The town’s name came from a community picnic, where the choice was made by drawing names out of a hat.

moments.title: Sunnyslope Wine Trail
moments.text: Sunnyslope is a center of the Snake River Valley American Viticultural Area, with 14 area wineries making up the Sunnyslope Wine Trail. State Highway 55 runs through the community.

moments.title: Map Rock
moments.text: Map Rock is a massive basalt boulder covered in petroglyphs. The district includes carvings believed to have been made by Northern Shoshone before 19th-century settlers expanded westward into Idaho. Robert Limbert gave it that name in the early 1920s because he believed the markings depicted the Snake River valley. In 1924, a proposal called for moving the rock, or cutting it into pieces, for display on the State Capitol grounds in Boise. The plan was abandoned, but the rock was found to have suffered damage. Canyon County acquired Map Rock and the surrounding 38 acres in 2012.
